items.stimulus: A city has 1,600 bus stops, and 400 of them are in the downtown district. Planners chose 80 of the downtown stops at random and found that 30% of the stops they chose had a covered shelter.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Approximately 30% of all bus stops in the city have a covered shelter.
Approximately 30% of bus stops in the downtown district have a covered shelter.
Approximately 70% of bus stops in the downtown district have a covered shelter.
Most of the bus stops in the downtown district have a covered shelter.
items.explanation: The planners only sampled downtown stops, so the 30% can only stand for the downtown district. Because the stops were chosen at random, you can carry the 30% over to all downtown stops, and you say 'approximately' because it is an estimate from a sample.

A.why: You applied the result to every stop in the city. No stops outside downtown were sampled, so the data say nothing about them.

C.why: 70% is the share of sampled stops that did NOT have a shelter. You reported the complement instead.

D.why: 30% is well under half, so the sample does not support a claim that most downtown stops have shelters.

Approximately 40% of all fish in the reserve have ingested microplastics.
A typical blue rockfish in the reserve has ingested about 40 microplastic pieces.
Approximately 40% of blue rockfish in all kelp forests have ingested microplastics.
items.explanation: 48 out of 120 is 40%. Only blue rockfish in this reserve were sampled at random, so the percent applies to that group alone: approximately 40% of blue rockfish in the reserve have ingested microplastics.

B.why: You applied the result to every species in the reserve. Only blue rockfish were sampled, and the other 30-plus species may feed in different ways.

C.why: You changed a percent of fish into a count of pieces per fish. The biologists recorded whether each fish had any microplastics, not how many pieces it held.

D.why: You used the right species but the wrong place. The fish all came from one reserve, so the result can't be applied to kelp forests elsewhere.

items.subtype_name: Which population can the sample speak for
items.stimulus: A quarry contains 3,500 fossil leaves, and 900 of them are from ginkgo trees. A paleobotanist selected 100 of the fossil ginkgo leaves at random and counted the insect feeding marks on each one. Of the leaves selected, 30% had more than 5 feeding marks.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Approximately 30% of all the fossil leaves in the quarry have more than 5 feeding marks.
Approximately 70% of the fossil ginkgo leaves in the quarry have more than 5 feeding marks.
Approximately 30% of the fossil ginkgo leaves in the quarry have more than 5 feeding marks.
The fossil ginkgo leaves in the quarry have an average of approximately 5 feeding marks each.
items.explanation: The 100 leaves were chosen at random from the 900 ginkgo leaves only, so the sample speaks for the ginkgo leaves in the quarry. You carry the same statistic over to that group: approximately 30% of them have more than 5 feeding marks.

A.why: You applied the result to all 3,500 leaves in the quarry, but only ginkgo leaves were sampled. The other 2,600 leaves come from different plants and could have very different amounts of damage.

B.why: 70% is the share of sampled leaves that did NOT have more than 5 feeding marks. You flipped the result to its complement.

D.why: The data give a percent above a threshold, not an average. Knowing that 30% of the leaves have more than 5 marks tells you nothing about the mean number of marks per leaf.

items.subtype_name: Which population can the sample speak for
items.stimulus: A regional archive holds 4,000 recorded folk songs, and 1,200 of them are sea shanties. A folklorist selected 150 of the sea shanties at random and found that 40% of the selected songs repeat their refrain more than 3 times.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Approximately 40% of the sea shanties in the archive repeat their refrain more than 3 times.
Approximately 40% of all the songs in the archive repeat their refrain more than 3 times.
Approximately 60% of the sea shanties in the archive repeat their refrain more than 3 times.
The sea shanties in the archive repeat their refrain an average of approximately 3 times.
items.explanation: The random sample was drawn only from the 1,200 sea shanties, so the conclusion can apply only to the sea shanties in the archive. Keep the same statistic, hedged: approximately 40% of them repeat their refrain more than 3 times.

B.why: You extended the result to all 4,000 songs, but no songs other than sea shanties were sampled. Ballads, lullabies and other kinds of songs may use refrains very differently.

C.why: 60% is the share of sampled shanties that do NOT repeat their refrain more than 3 times. You reported the complement instead of the share asked about.

D.why: You turned a percent above a threshold into an average. Knowing how many songs pass 3 repetitions does not tell you the mean number of repetitions.

items.subtype_name: Which population can the sample speak for
items.stimulus: Excavators at a site recovered 6,000 pottery sherds, and 2,400 of them are red-slip ware. The others are plain ware. An archaeologist selected 80 of the red-slip sherds at random and found that 20 of the selected sherds show traces of soot.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Approximately 25% of all the sherds recovered from the site show traces of soot.
Approximately 25% of the plain sherds recovered from the site show traces of soot.
Approximately 20% of the red-slip sherds recovered from the site show traces of soot.
Approximately 25% of the red-slip sherds recovered from the site show traces of soot.
items.explanation: First convert the count to a percent: $\frac{20}{80} = 0.25$, or 25%. The sample was drawn only from the red-slip sherds, so the conclusion applies only to them: approximately 25% of the red-slip sherds from the site show soot.

A.why: You applied the result to all 6,000 sherds, but the plain-ware sherds were never sampled. The sample can speak only for the red-slip sherds.

B.why: You moved the result over to the plain sherds, which is a group that was never sampled. The 25% figure comes from red-slip sherds and says nothing about plain ware.

C.why: You read 20, the number of sooty sherds, as if it were a percent. Twenty out of 80 is 25%, not 20%.
